knowledge.title: Daily prayer in Somali life (Salaadda shanta waqti)
knowledge.text:
The five daily prayers (salaad, plural salaado) structure the Somali day. Their Somali names are: Subax (dawn, Fajr), Duhur (midday, Dhuhr), Casar (afternoon, Asr), Maqrib (sunset, Maghrib) and Cishe (night, Isha). Somalis say "salaadda tukasho" for performing prayer (tukasho = praying) and "waqtigii salaadda" for prayer time. The call to prayer is the aadaan, and the person who calls it is the mu'addin (Somali: mu'adin or aadaamiye). Before praying, one performs ablution, weysa (wudu'). Friday congregational prayer is salaadda Jimcaha, and Friday (Jimce) is the weekly day off in Somalia, with many offices also closed or working half-day on Thursday.

Prayer times shift through the year and by location, but because Somalia lies close to the equator the variation is small: in Mogadishu, Fajr is roughly 4:30–5:00 am and Maghrib roughly 5:50–6:20 pm local time (EAT, UTC+3) year-round. In the far north (Hargeysa, Boosaaso) the variation is a little larger. Somalia uses East Africa Time (UTC+3) with no daylight saving. Following the Shafi'i school, Asr begins when an object's shadow equals its own length (plus its noon shadow). An assistant asked for exact times should compute them for the user's city and date, or say that local mosque timetables are authoritative, rather than guess.

Etiquette and practice: shops often close briefly at prayer times, especially for Jimce midday prayer; men commonly pray in the mosque (masjid), women more often at home, though many mosques have women's sections. Prayer mats (sallaad or masalle) are found in homes, offices and even at roadside stops. Travellers may shorten and combine prayers (qasar and jamac). It is polite not to walk directly in front of someone praying and to keep noise down during the aadaan. A meeting or call is often paused with "waqtigii salaadda waa la gaaray" (it is prayer time).

For an assistant: when scheduling, avoid setting calls or reminders during Jimce prayer (around 12:00–13:30 on Fridays) and at Maghrib in Ramadan. If a user asks for reminders, offer prayer-time reminders tied to their city. Do not lecture users about their prayer habits; answer questions about how to pray factually according to the Shafi'i school unless the user asks about another school.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salah; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shafi%CA%BBi_school; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_Somalia; https://www.islamicfinder.org/world/somalia/53654/mogadishu-prayer-times/

knowledge.title: Ramadan in Somalia (Bisha Soonka / Ramadaan)
knowledge.text:
Ramadan (Somali: Ramadaan or Ramadaan Kariim; the month is also called bisha soonka, "the month of fasting") is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar. Fasting is soon or soomid; to fast is "soomaya". It begins and ends with the sighting of the new moon (bil), and in Somalia the start is announced by religious authorities and the government; occasionally Somalia, Somaliland and diaspora communities begin a day apart, which is a common topic of conversation.

Daily rhythm: before dawn families eat suxuur (suhoor), often canjeero/laxoox, rice or porridge with tea. At sunset, at the Maqrib aadaan, the fast is broken (afur, iftar), traditionally with dates (timir) and water, followed by sambuusa, bajiye, fruit juice and tea, then the Maqrib prayer and a larger meal later. Mosques fill for the night prayer tarawiix (tarawih), and many people try to complete reading the whole Qur'an (khatmi) during the month. The last ten nights are especially important; the 27th night is popularly observed as Laylatul Qadr (Habeenka Qadarka).

Social life: working hours shorten; markets and streets come alive after afur; charity increases. Before Eid, every Muslim who can must give Sakada Fidriga (zakat al-fitr), traditionally a measure of grain or its value in money, given to the poor. Many people also pay their annual zakat (sako) in Ramadan. Diaspora relatives send extra remittances for Ramadan and Eid, and mobile money transfers peak at this time.

Greetings: "Ramadaan Kariim" or "Ramadaan Mubaarak" at the start; "Soon wanaagsan" (have a good fast); "Allaha naga aqbalo" (may God accept it from us). Asking "ma soomantahay?" (are you fasting?) is common among friends but should not be used to judge. People exempt from fasting include the sick, travellers, pregnant or nursing women and those menstruating, and they make up days later or give fidya, according to Islamic rules.

Upcoming dates (approximate; final dates depend on moon sighting): Ramadan 1448 AH is expected to begin around 8 February 2027, with Eid al-Fitr around 9–10 March 2027. Ramadan 1447 began around 18–19 February 2026, with Eid al-Fitr on 20–21 March 2026.

Assistant behaviour in Ramadan: greet users with Ramadan greetings, shift suggested meal or meeting times around suxuur and afur, avoid food-heavy small talk during fasting hours unless asked, and offer accurate suxuur/afur times for the user's city when asked.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramadan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zakat_al-Fitr; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_in_Somalia; https://www.timeanddate.com/holidays/somalia/

knowledge.title: Eid customs in Somalia (Ciidda Soonfur iyo Ciidda Carrafo / Ciid al-Adxa)
knowledge.text:
Somalis celebrate two Eids. Ciidda Soonfur (Eid al-Fitr, "the Eid of breaking the fast") marks the end of Ramadan on 1 Shawwal. Ciidda Carrafo or Ciid al-Adxa (Eid al-Adha, also Ciidda Weyn) falls on 10 Dhul Hijja, the day after the Day of Arafah (Maalinta Carrafo) during the Hajj. Both are public holidays in Somalia and Somaliland; the government usually announces one to three days off.

Typical Eid morning: people bathe, put on new clothes (dharka ciidda), and go early to the Eid prayer (salaadda ciidda), often held in large open grounds or stadiums as well as mosques. Before Ciidda Soonfur prayer, zakat al-fitr must already have been given. Children receive new clothes and Eid money (lacagta ciidda), and women and girls often decorate hands and feet with henna (xinna) the night before. Families prepare xalwo (Somali halwa), cookies (buskud), cambuulo, rice and meat dishes, and serve tea and coffee to a steady stream of visitors. Visiting relatives and elders, reconciling disputes, and remembering the poor are core parts of the day.

Ciidda Carrafo is associated with the animal sacrifice (udxiyo, from Arabic udhiya; also called "neef la gowraco"): those able to afford it slaughter a goat, sheep, cow or camel after the Eid prayer and share the meat between family, neighbours and the poor. Livestock prices rise sharply before this Eid, and the season is also the peak for Somali livestock exports to Saudi Arabia for Hajj, through Berbera and Boosaaso ports. Many people fast on the Day of Arafah.

Greetings: "Ciid wanaagsan" (good Eid), "Ciid Mubaarak", "Ciid farxad leh" (a happy Eid), and the reply "Adiga iyo qoyskaagaba" or "Sannad walba adigoo nabad qaba" (may you be well every year). "Ciiddiin wanaagsan" is the plural form.

Recent and expected dates (approximate; depend on moon sighting): Eid al-Fitr 2026 was 20–21 March 2026 and Eid al-Adha 2026 was 27–28 May 2026. Eid al-Fitr 2027 is expected around 9–10 March 2027 and Eid al-Adha 2027 around 16–17 May 2027 (as of October 2026).

For an assistant: send warm Eid greetings in Somali on Eid days, be aware that business and government services slow for several days, and do not assume every user can afford a sacrifice or new clothes.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eid_al-Fitr; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eid_al-Adha; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_in_Somalia; https://www.timeanddate.com/holidays/somalia/

knowledge.title: Mawlid and other religious occasions (Mawliidka, Isra' iyo Mi'raaj, Sannadka Hijriga)
knowledge.text:
Mawliid (Mawlid an-Nabi) commemorates the birth of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), celebrated on 12 Rabi' al-Awwal of the Islamic calendar. In Somalia it is widely observed, especially by Sufi-affiliated communities: people gather in mosques, homes and tents to recite praise poetry (madax, qasiido, the Barzanji and the Burda), perform dikri, and share food such as rice, meat and halwa. In some places celebrations continue through the whole month of Rabi' al-Awwal ("bisha Mawliidka"). Some reformist scholars consider Mawlid celebrations an innovation, so attitudes differ between families; an assistant should simply describe the custom and not argue for or against it. Mawlid has been listed as a public holiday in Somalia. In 2026 it fell around 26 August; in 2027 it is expected around 15 August (approximate, depends on the moon).

Other religious days observed in Somalia:
- Isra' iyo Mi'raaj (27 Rajab): the Night Journey and Ascension of the Prophet; listed as a public holiday (around 16 January 2026; around 6 January 2027).
- Sannadka Cusub ee Hijriga (1 Muharram), the Islamic New Year (around 17 June 2026; around 6 June 2027).
- Caashuuro (Ashura, 10 Muharram): many Somalis fast on this day, following Sunni tradition.
- Laylatul Qadr (Habeenka Qadarka), in the last ten nights of Ramadan.
- Maalinta Carrafo (Day of Arafah, 9 Dhul Hijja), a recommended fast for those not on Hajj.
- Every Monday and Thursday some people fast voluntarily (soonka Isniinta iyo Khamiista), and the "white days" (13–15 of each lunar month).

Hajj (Xajka) and Umra (Cumra) are major aspirations; a person who has performed Hajj is called Xaaji (man) or Xaajiyad/Xaajo (woman), a respected title used in address, e.g. "Xaaji Cali". Hajj travel is organised through licensed agencies and the Ministry of Religious Affairs, with quotas set by Saudi Arabia.

Dates in the Islamic calendar move about 10–11 days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar, so the assistant should always give Gregorian equivalents as approximate unless confirmed by an official announcement.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mawlid; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra%27_and_Mi%27raj

knowledge.title: Common Islamic phrases and duas in Somali speech and when to use them
knowledge.text:
Arabic religious phrases, adapted to Somali pronunciation and spelling, are used constantly in Somali conversation. Using them correctly makes an assistant sound natural and respectful.

Greetings: "Assalaamu calaykum" (peace be upon you) is the standard greeting; the reply is "Wacalaykum assalaam" (and upon you peace), often extended to "...wa raxmatullaahi wa barakaatuh". Somali "nabad" (peace) greetings follow: "Iska warran?", "Nabad miyaa?" (Is it peace?), reply "Waa nabad" or "Nabad".

Everyday phrases:
- Bismillaah (in the name of God): before eating, drinking, starting work, a journey or a task.
- Alxamdulillaah (praise be to God): after eating, when asked "how are you?" ("Waan fiicanahay, Alxamdulillaah"), after good news or even after hardship.
- Insha Allah / In shaa Allaah (if God wills): when speaking of any future plan. A promise without it can sound presumptuous.
- Mashaa Allah (what God has willed): when admiring a child, a house, success, to avoid envy or the evil eye (il).
- Subxaanallaah (glory be to God): in amazement or surprise.
- Allaahu akbar (God is greatest): in prayer, in awe or at major news.
- Astaghfirullaah (I seek God's forgiveness): after a mistake or on hearing something improper.
- Jazaakallaahu khayran (may God reward you with good): a strong "thank you"; Somali alternatives: "Mahadsanid" (thank you, singular), "Mahadsanidiin" (plural), "Ilaahay ha ku barakeeyo" (God bless you).
- Inna lillaahi wa inna ilayhi raajicuun (to God we belong and to Him we return): on hearing of a death or a loss.
- Allaha u naxariisto (may God have mercy on him/her): said after mentioning a deceased person, like "the late".
- Ilaahay ha ku caafiyo / Allaha ku caafiyo (may God grant you health): to a sick person or after someone's effort; also a polite "no, thank you" when declining food.
- Ilaahay ha idin barakeeyo: to a newly married couple or a family.
- Aamiin (amen): response to any dua.
- Haddii Alle idmo: Somali equivalent of "God willing".

Duco (dua, supplication) is made for travellers ("Safar nabadeed" — have a safe journey; "Alle ha ku dhowro"), for exam takers, for the sick and for the dead. Ending a conversation with "Nabad gelyo" (go in peace) or "Ilaahay ha ku ilaaliyo" (God protect you) is warm and natural.

Assistant guidance: use these phrases naturally, not excessively; mirror the user's level of religious language; always say "Allaha u naxariisto" after naming someone who has died; and never use religious phrases jokingly or sarcastically.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_honorifics; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_language; https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php

knowledge.title: Death, funerals and mourning customs (Geeri, aas iyo tacsi)
knowledge.text:
Somali funeral practice follows Islamic rules closely, with Somali social customs around mourning and condolence.

When someone dies: those present say "Inna lillaahi wa inna ilayhi raajicuun". News spreads fast by phone, radio announcements, and social media (Facebook, WhatsApp, TikTok) with the formula "...ayaa geeriyooday / ku geeriyooday..." (has passed away) and "Allaha u naxariisto". Burial (aas) takes place as quickly as possible, usually the same day or within 24 hours. The body is washed (maydhid, ghusl) by people of the same gender, wrapped in white cloth (kafan or kafan cad), and the funeral prayer, salaadda janaasada, is performed in a mosque or open ground. Men carry the body to the cemetery (xabaal, qabri; cemetery: xabaalo/qabuuro), and burial is in the ground facing the qibla, without a coffin in Somalia. Traditionally men attend the burial; women mourn at home. In the diaspora, funerals follow local law, and families sometimes repatriate the body, which is costly and organised through community funds.

Tacsi (condolence): for about three days the family receives visitors at home or in a tent. Visitors say "Allaha u naxariisto", "Ilaahay samir iyo iimaan ha idinka siiyo" (may God give you patience and faith), or "Ilaahay jannadii ha ka waraabiyo" (may God give him/her drink in paradise). Neighbours and relatives bring food, cook for the family, and contribute money (often via mobile money) towards funeral costs. Gatherings recite the Qur'an (khatmi) and make duco for the deceased; some families hold a religious gathering and meal on the third, seventh or fortieth day (e.g. "toddobaad", "afartan"), though some reformist scholars discourage fixed-day rituals. Widows observe the Islamic waiting period (cidda / ciddo) of four months and ten days, wearing modest clothing and limiting outings.

Etiquette: speak softly, avoid jokes, do not ask intrusive questions about the cause of death, and avoid speaking ill of the deceased. Sending condolence by phone or message is normal: "Tacsi: Allaha u naxariisto [name], Ilaahay samir iyo iimaan ha idin siiyo, jannada ha ka waraabiyo."

Assistant behaviour: when a user mentions a death, respond first with "Inna lillaahi wa inna ilayhi raajicuun, Allaha u naxariisto" and genuine sympathy, offer practical help (drafting a condolence message, a death announcement, or explaining steps), and keep the rest of the reply short and gentle. Do not discuss inheritance (dhaxal) unless asked; if asked, explain that Islamic inheritance shares apply and recommend a qualified sheikh or lawyer.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_funeral; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iddah; https://ethnomed.org/culture/somali/; https://culturalatlas.sbs.com.au/somali-culture

knowledge.title: Public holidays in Somalia and Somaliland (Fasaxyada qaranka)
knowledge.text:
Somalia's official public holidays combine fixed civic dates with Islamic holidays that follow the lunar calendar.

Fixed civic holidays (Federal Republic of Somalia):
- 1 January: New Year's Day (Sannad Cusub).
- 1 May: Labour Day (Maalinta Shaqaalaha).
- 26 June: Independence of the former British Somaliland (Xorriyadda Waqooyi), which became independent as the State of Somaliland on 26 June 1960.
- 1 July: Independence and Union Day (Maalinta Xorriyadda iyo Midnimada), when the Trust Territory of Somalia (former Italian Somaliland) became independent and united with the State of Somaliland on 1 July 1960 to form the Somali Republic. The week of 26 June–1 July is celebrated as "Toddobaadka Xorriyadda" with flags, music and events. The Somali flag (calanka buluugga ah, a white five-pointed star on light blue) was first raised on 12 October 1954, which is marked as Flag Day (Maalinta Calanka).

Islamic holidays (dates shift about 11 days earlier each year): Isra' iyo Mi'raaj; Ciidda Soonfur (Eid al-Fitr, usually 1–3 days off); Ciidda Carrafo (Eid al-Adha, usually 2–3 days off); Islamic New Year (1 Muharram); Ashura (10 Muharram); and Mawliid (12 Rabi' al-Awwal). The government announces exact days off shortly before each holiday.

Approximate 2026 dates: Isra' and Mi'raj 16 January; Eid al-Fitr 20–21 March; Eid al-Adha 27–28 May; Islamic New Year 17 June; Ashura 26 June; Mawlid 26 August. Approximate 2027 dates (as of October 2026, subject to moon sighting): Isra' and Mi'raj ~6 January; Eid al-Fitr ~9–10 March; Eid al-Adha ~16–17 May; Islamic New Year ~6 June; Ashura ~15 June; Mawlid ~15 August.

Somaliland's holidays: Somaliland celebrates 18 May as its "Restoration of Sovereignty" or National Day (Maalinta 18 May), marking its 1991 declaration, and 26 June as its independence day; it does not celebrate 1 July as a union day. Puntland marks 1 August, the founding of Puntland State in 1998.

Former holiday: under Siad Barre, 21 October (the 1969 coup, "Kacaanka") was a major national holiday; it is no longer an official holiday in Somalia.

Weekend: Friday (Jimce) is the official weekly rest day; many offices close or work half-day on Thursday (Khamiis). For an assistant: check whether a date is a holiday before promising government or bank service, and give Islamic holiday dates as approximate.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somaliland

knowledge.title: The Somali traditional calendar and seasons (Xilliyada sannadka: Gu', Xagaa, Dayr, Jiilaal)
knowledge.text:
Somali pastoral life follows four seasons defined by rain, not by temperature. The traditional names are used throughout Somalia, Somaliland, Djibouti and the Somali regions of Ethiopia and Kenya.

1. Gu' (roughly April–June): the main rainy season. Pasture and water return, camels and goats give milk, and it is the main planting season in the farming areas of the Jubba and Shabeelle valleys and the Bay region. A good Gu' is celebrated; a failed Gu' (gu' la'aan) leads to drought (abaar). Weddings and gatherings were traditionally common after good rains.
2. Xagaa (roughly July–September): the cool, dry season of the strong south-west monsoon. Inland it is dry and windy; along the southern coast there are light showers (the "xagaa rains"). In the north-east, especially Boosaaso and Berbera on the Gulf of Aden coast, this is the hottest time, with very high temperatures and hot winds (the "khariif" wind in the north).
3. Dayr (roughly October–December): the second, shorter rainy season, sometimes called the "short rains". Dayr rains are less reliable than Gu'. Planting of a second crop occurs in the riverine and agro-pastoral areas.
4. Jiilaal (roughly December/January–March): the harsh dry season, hottest and driest in most of the country, when pastoralists move herds to permanent wells and water prices rise. It is considered the hardest time of the year for herders.

Rain timing varies by region and year, and climate change has made seasons more erratic; Somalia experienced a historic five consecutive failed rainy seasons in 2020–2023, followed by severe flooding linked to El Niño in late 2023. Agencies such as FAO-SWALIM and FSNAU issue Gu' and Dayr seasonal forecasts and assessments.

Traditional solar calendar: Somali herders also reckoned time using a solar year and star-based knowledge. Experts called "xiddigiye" (astronomers) tracked the stars and lunar mansions to predict rains. The traditional Somali New Year was marked by Dabshid (literally "fire lighting"), a festival held in late July, when people lit bonfires and jumped over fire; in Afgooye it was associated with Istunka, the famous stick-fighting festival. Days of the week in Somali are: Isniin (Monday), Talaado (Tuesday), Arbaco (Wednesday), Khamiis (Thursday), Jimce (Friday), Sabti (Saturday), Axad (Sunday).

For an assistant: when discussing farming, livestock, weather or drought, use the season names; describe current conditions only from fresh sources (e.g. FAO-SWALIM, FSNAU, Somali Disaster Management Agency).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istunka; https://www.faoswalim.org/; https://fsnau.org/

knowledge.title: The Islamic (Hijri) calendar in Somalia (Taariikhda Hijriga)
knowledge.text:
Somalis use two calendars side by side: the Gregorian calendar for government, business, school and international dealings, and the Islamic Hijri calendar (taariikhda Hijriga) for religious life. The Hijri calendar is purely lunar: 12 months of 29 or 30 days, about 354–355 days in total, so Islamic dates move roughly 10–11 days earlier each Gregorian year. Year 1 AH began with the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. As of October 2026 the Hijri year is 1448 AH (1 Muharram 1448 fell around 17 June 2026).

The months, with Somali usage and key events:
1. Muxarram (Muharram): Islamic New Year; Caashuuro on the 10th.
2. Safar.
3. Rabiicul Awwal: Mawliid on the 12th; often called "bisha Mawliidka".
4. Rabiicul Aakhir.
5. Jumaadal Uulaa.
6. Jumaadal Aakhira.
7. Rajab: Isra' iyo Mi'raaj on the 27th.
8. Shacbaan (Sha'ban): preparation for Ramadan.
9. Ramadaan: the fasting month.
10. Shawwaal: Ciidda Soonfur on the 1st; six optional fast days (lixda Shawwaal).
11. Dul Qacda (Dhul Qa'da).
12. Dul Xijja (Dhul Hijja): Hajj; Maalinta Carrafo on the 9th; Ciidda Carrafo on the 10th.

Traditional Somali also has its own names for some lunar months that elders still use, especially in pastoral areas: for example the month after Ramadan is called "bisha Soonfurka" (Shawwal) and the Hajj month "bisha Carrafo" (Dhul Hijja). Other traditional month names vary by region and dialect, so the assistant should prefer the standard Arabic-derived names unless the user uses the traditional ones, and should not guess a traditional name it is unsure of.

Moon sighting: months begin when the new crescent (bisha cusub) is sighted. In Somalia, official announcements come from the Ministry of Religious Affairs and scholars, sometimes following Saudi Arabia's announcement and sometimes local sighting, so there can be a one-day difference between Somalia, Somaliland, Djibouti and diaspora communities.

Practical guidance for an assistant: when giving a Hijri date, state the Gregorian equivalent and say it may differ by one day depending on local announcement. Use code (e.g. a conversion library) rather than mental arithmetic for conversions. When a user writes a date like "15 Ramadaan", answer in both calendars.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_in_Somalia

knowledge.title: Somali family structure (Qoyska iyo xigaalada)
knowledge.text:
The family (qoys) is the centre of Somali social life, and the wider kin network (qaraabo, ehel) is a source of identity, protection and obligation. Families are traditionally patrilineal: a child belongs to the father's lineage, and Somali names reflect this. A person's full name is their own given name followed by their father's and grandfather's names, e.g. Cabdi Maxamed Faarax = Cabdi, son of Maxamed, son of Faarax. Women keep their own father's name after marriage; a wife does not take her husband's name, so mothers and children have different "surnames", which matters for forms, passports and travel bookings abroad.

Kinship terms: aabbe (father), hooyo (mother), walaal (sibling; walaalkay = my brother, walaashay = my sister), adeer (paternal uncle, also used for any older man), eedo (paternal aunt), abti (maternal uncle), habaryar (maternal aunt; literally "little mother"), awoowe (grandfather), ayeeyo (grandmother), ina-adeer (paternal cousin), seeddi (brother-in-law, husband's or wife's brother), soddog / soddoh (father-/mother-in-law). The maternal side (reer abti) has special affection: the abti is a protective, indulgent figure.

Household: many Somali households are extended, with grandparents, unmarried siblings or relatives' children living together. Large families are common; Somalia has one of the highest fertility rates in the world (around 6 children per woman in recent UN estimates). Children are expected to help at home, respect elders and, as adults, support parents financially. Remittances (xawaalad) from relatives abroad are a family duty; many households depend on them.

Roles: traditionally the father is the provider and public representative of the household, and the mother runs the home and raises children, while also often running small businesses and markets. In practice, since the civil war many women have become main breadwinners. Polygyny (up to four wives under Islamic law) is legal and practised by a minority.

Family obligations extend to the lineage: relatives contribute to weddings, funerals, medical bills, school fees and blood compensation (mag). Asking for help from relatives is normal and not shameful, and refusing without reason can damage relationships.

Assistant guidance: when filling forms or booking travel, explain that a Somali woman's last name is her father's name; ask for the name exactly as in the passport. Use kinship terms warmly ("adeer", "eedo", "walaal") as Somalis do, and never make jokes about someone's mother or family.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_people; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_name; https://culturalatlas.sbs.com.au/somali-culture; https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.TFRT.IN?locations=SO

knowledge.title: Respect for elders and social etiquette (Ixtiraamka waayeelka iyo edebta)
knowledge.text:
Respect (ixtiraam, sharaf) for elders, parents and guests is one of the most emphasised Somali values. Good manners are called "edeb" or "anshax", and a well-behaved person is "edeb leh". Elders (waayeel; odayaal for clan elders) are listened to, given the best seat and served first, and their advice is sought in disputes.

Forms of address: younger people address older men as "adeer" (uncle) or "aabbe" and older women as "eedo" (aunt) or "hooyo" (mother), even when not related. Peers call each other "walaal" (brother/sister). Respected titles include Xaaji/Xaajiyad (someone who did Hajj), Sheekh (a religious scholar), Macallin/Macallimad (teacher), Dhakhtar (doctor), Ugaas, Suldaan, Garaad, Boqor and Islaan (traditional clan leaders' titles, which vary by region). Many people are known by nicknames (naanays), e.g. "Cali Dheere" (tall Ali), "Faarax Yare"; these are normal and not insulting.

Etiquette points:
- Greetings are long and important: ask after health, family and news before business ("Iska warran? Caafimaad? Qoyska ma nabad baa?").
- Use the right hand for eating, giving and receiving.
- Don't sit with soles of the feet facing an elder or put your feet up in their presence.
- Physical contact between unrelated men and women, including handshakes, is avoided by many religious Somalis; wait for the other person to offer a hand.
- Speak modestly about oneself; boasting is disliked, and praise should be accompanied by "Mashaa Allah".
- Interrupting or contradicting an elder in public is rude; disagreement is expressed indirectly, often through a proverb (maahmaah).
- Swearing, mentioning sexual topics and insulting someone's mother or lineage are serious offences.

Hospitality: guests (martida) are honoured; a visitor is offered tea, food and if needed a place to sleep, and refusing the offer outright can offend. Saying "soo dhawoow" (welcome; plural "soo dhawaada") is standard.

Elder care: caring for aging parents is considered a religious and moral duty (waalid u wanaajin); nursing homes are rare and seen as shameful by many, even in the diaspora.

Assistant guidance: be polite and slightly formal by default, especially in voice calls; if a user appears older, use respectful forms ("adeer", "hooyo" only if the user invites it, otherwise neutral polite "mudane" for sir, "marwo" for madam). Never mock elders, traditional titles or religious figures.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Somalia; https://culturalatlas.sbs.com.au/somali-culture; https://ethnomed.org/culture/somali/

knowledge.title: The Somali marriage process: guurdoon, gabbaati, meher, yarad, nikaax (Habka guurka)
knowledge.text:
Somali marriage combines the Islamic marriage contract with customary steps that vary by region, clan and family. Common patterns:

1. Guurdoon / doon (seeking a spouse; "guur" = marriage, "doon" = seek): today most couples meet through family, school, work, social media or friends; the families then become involved. Arranged and family-introduced marriages remain common, but Islamic law and Somali Family Law require the consent of the bride. A man formally "asks for" a woman ("gabadh doonasho" / "soo doonid").

2. Gabbaati: the gift the groom and his father or relatives bring when they first come to ask for the bride's hand. Traditionally it was a young camel; today it is usually money or gifts to the bride's immediate family, as a gesture of respect.

3. Yarad: the main bride-wealth, money and gifts (historically camels) that the groom's family gives to the bride's family, negotiated by elders before the wedding. It is a cultural custom, not an Islamic requirement, and amounts vary widely with social standing. Sooryo: smaller gifts or money for the bride's male relatives. In return, the bride's family traditionally gives dibaad: household goods, furnishings and sometimes livestock to help the couple set up their home.

4. Meher (mahr): the Islamic marriage gift the groom gives to the bride herself. It is obligatory in Islam, belongs only to her, and can be paid immediately or deferred. It is agreed and stated at the contract.

5. Nikaax (nikah, the Islamic contract): performed by a sheikh with the bride's guardian (wali, usually her father; Somali "walii"), the groom, two witnesses and the agreed meher. It may happen days or months before the wedding celebration, sometimes in a mosque.

6. Aroos (the wedding celebration) and the customs that follow it: see the separate entry on weddings (aroos, xeedho, shaash saar).

Modern realities: wedding costs (yarad, gold, venue, clothes) are a major financial burden and a frequent topic; many scholars and community leaders encourage simpler, cheaper weddings. Urban couples often skip or reduce yarad and gabbaati. Elopement (masaafo / "la-tag") happens when families disagree and is later regularised through elders. Somalia's 1975 Family Law set rules on consent, minimum age and divorce, though in practice religious and customary law dominate.

Assistant guidance: explain these steps neutrally as common patterns that differ by family and region; distinguish clearly between meher (Islamic, to the bride) and yarad (customary, to her family); do not give personal religious rulings and suggest a sheikh for contract questions.
Sources: https://somalimarriage.com/glossary; https://somalimarriage.com/guides/somali-marriage-payments; https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/llglrd/2019671091/2019671091.pdf; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahr

knowledge.title: Somali weddings: aroos, xeedho, shaash saar and celebrations (Arooska Soomaaliyeed)
knowledge.text:
The aroos (wedding celebration) usually follows the nikaax (Islamic contract). In cities it is typically held in a wedding hall or hotel, often in the evening, and many weddings have separate or partly separate celebrations for men and women.

Typical elements:
- Dress: the bride often wears a white Western-style wedding gown for the main party, and also traditional dress such as the dirac (a long, light, flowing dress worn over a gorgorad underskirt), the guntiino (a draped cloth worn over one shoulder), and the garbasaar (shawl). Gold jewellery (dahab) given by the groom is important. The night before, women hold a henna night (habeenka xinnaha) where the bride's hands and feet are decorated.
- Music and dance: live bands or DJs play Somali songs; traditional dances such as dhaanto (associated with the north and Ethiopia's Somali Region), niiko (southern, with rhythmic hip movement), and regional group dances are performed. Women sing buraanbur praise poetry for the bride and families.
- Food: rice (bariis), goat or camel meat, pasta, sambuusa, juice and the sweet xalwo.
- Shaash saar ("placing the headscarf"): usually on the seventh day after the wedding or soon after, married women of the family place a shaash (headscarf) on the bride's head, symbolising her new status as a married woman, accompanied by buraanbur and celebration. The groom's family may give gifts at this event.
- Xeedho: a decorated container prepared by the bride's mother and female relatives, filled with muqmad/oodkac (small pieces of dried camel meat fried and preserved in ghee) and dates, wrapped in layers of cloth and tied with hidden knots. The groom's side must open it, sometimes reciting poetry or solving the knot puzzle, a playful test of honour between the families. UNESCO recognised the xeedho tradition of Djibouti as intangible cultural heritage.
- Aqal gal / toddoba bax: traditionally the couple spends the first seven days at home ("todobada"), receiving visitors and food; "todoba bax" marks the end of that week.

Many customs are optional and differ greatly between north and south, rural and urban, and in the diaspora, where weddings often blend Somali and local customs. Greetings for the couple: "Aroos wanaagsan", "Ilaahay ha idiin barakeeyo, ha idin waafajiyo" (God bless and harmonise you), "Ilaahay ha idinku nasiibiyo carruur wanaagsan" (may God bless you with good children).

Assistant guidance: describe these as common customs, not fixed rules; offer to draft wedding invitations or congratulation messages in Somali; avoid commenting on wedding costs unless asked.
Sources: https://somalimarriage.com/guides/somali-wedding-traditions-aroos; https://ich.unesco.org/en/USL/xeedho-02001; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac; https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/eoir/legacy/2013/06/11/arranged%20marriage.pdf

knowledge.title: Birth and naming a newborn (Dhalashada iyo magac bixinta)
knowledge.text:
The birth of a child is celebrated with congratulations ("Hambalyo!", "Ilaahay ha idiin barakeeyo ilmaha", "Ilmo khayr leh ha noqdo" - may the child be blessed), visits and food. Common customs include:

- Afar-tanka / umul: the new mother (umul) traditionally rests for about 40 days (afartan maalmood) after birth, cared for by her mother, sisters and female relatives, who cook nourishing food such as soup, porridge (mishaari/boorash), meat and milk, and handle household duties. Visitors bring gifts and money.
- Aadaan: a relative, usually the father or a respected elder, may recite the aadaan (call to prayer) softly in the baby's ear soon after birth.
- Magac bixin (naming): the child is often named on the seventh day (toddobada), sometimes earlier, together with the cuqiiqo (aqiqah), the Islamic practice of slaughtering one or two goats or sheep and sharing the meat, and shaving the baby's hair. Some families do this later if they cannot afford it immediately.
- Naming practice: the given name is followed by the father's and grandfather's names, so the "surname" changes each generation. Popular boys' names include Maxamed, Cabdullaahi, Axmed, Cali, Xasan, Xuseen, Yuusuf, Ibraahim, Cumar, Cabdiraxmaan, Mustafe and Somali names such as Guuleed (victorious), Geedi, Warsame (bringer of good news), Abshir (good tidings), Liibaan (success), Nuur. Popular girls' names include Faadumo, Caasha, Khadiija, Maryan, Xaliimo, Amina, Sahra, Hodan (wealth), Ayaan (luck), Ubax (flower), Ifrah (joy), Nasra, Sagal (a star), Hibaaq, Ugbaad, Deeqa (generous gift), Barwaaqo (prosperity), Hamdi.
- Some Somali names describe the circumstances of birth, e.g. Roble (born in the rain, from "roob"). Twins are often given paired names such as Xasan and Xuseen (boys) or Aadan and Xaawo (boy and girl).
- Nicknames (naanays) are given later in life based on appearance or character.

In the diaspora, naming on official documents requires care: the child's legal surname in many countries is the father's first name, and Somali names have many spellings in Latin script outside the official orthography (e.g. Mohamed/Maxamed, Hassan/Xasan, Fadumo/Faadumo, Abdi/Cabdi).

Assistant guidance: congratulate warmly; if asked for name ideas, offer Somali and Islamic names with meanings and give official Somali spelling plus common English spelling. Do not comment on the number of children or the baby's gender preference.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_name; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqiqah; https://ethnomed.org/culture/somali/; https://culturalatlas.sbs.com.au/somali-culture

knowledge.title: Gender roles in Somali society (Doorarka ragga iyo dumarka)
knowledge.text:
Somali society has traditionally assigned different roles to men and women, shaped by pastoral life, Islam and custom. These roles are changing, especially in cities and the diaspora. This entry describes them neutrally.

Traditional patterns: in pastoral life men cared for camels and cattle, handled clan politics, defence and negotiation, and elders who sit in the shir (council) were men. Women managed the home and children, cared for sheep and goats, built and dismantled the portable nomadic hut (aqal), and processed milk and food. Women have long been active in trade: market women selling milk, khat, food, cloth and gold are a familiar sight, and many women run businesses, money transfer shops and restaurants.

Change since 1991: the civil war killed and displaced many men, and women increasingly became breadwinners, peace activists and businesswomen. Women's organisations played major roles in peace conferences. Somalia's political system set a target of 30% of parliamentary seats for women; in practice women held around 24% of federal parliament seats after the 2016–2017 selection and around 20% after the 2021–2022 process. Women have served as ministers, including foreign minister (Fowsiyo Yuusuf Xaaji Aadan was the first female foreign minister, 2012–2014) and deputy prime minister. In Somaliland, women's representation in elected bodies has been very low.

Education and work: girls' school enrolment is lower than boys', especially in rural areas, but women are increasingly visible in universities, medicine, journalism and technology.

Dress: most Somali women wear the hijab or headscarf (masar, garbasaar, jilbaab, xijaab), and many wear long dresses (dirac, cabaayad/abaya). Men often wear the macawis (sarong) with a shirt, or Western clothes, and older men may wear the koofiyad (cap).

Sensitive issues: female genital cutting (gudniinka fircooniga / gudniin) has been extremely widespread in Somalia (prevalence among women 15–49 estimated around 99% in the 2020 Somali Health and Demographic Survey); there is active advocacy against it, and debate between the "pharaonic" and the "sunna" forms. Gender-based violence, early marriage and inheritance rights are also discussed by Somali activists.

Assistant guidance: treat men and women users equally and respectfully; avoid stereotypes ("Somali women are…"); do not lecture about religion or culture; answer questions on sensitive health topics such as FGM factually, compassionately and with health-service referrals; respect a user's preference for modest language.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Female_genital_mutilation_in_Somalia; https://somalia.unfpa.org/en/publications/somali-health-and-demographic-survey-2020; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowsiyo_Yuusuf_Xaaji_Aadan

knowledge.title: Somali diaspora life (Qurbajoogta Soomaaliyeed)
knowledge.text:
Somalis abroad are called qurbajoog (plural qurbajoogta; "qurbo" = abroad, exile). There are an estimated 1.5–2 million or more Somalis living outside the Horn of Africa, a diaspora that grew mainly after the civil war began in 1988–1991.

Main communities: Kenya (Eastleigh in Nairobi, plus refugee camps at Dadaab and Kakuma), Ethiopia, Yemen, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt, Uganda (Kampala), South Africa, the United States (especially Minneapolis–Saint Paul in Minnesota, Columbus in Ohio, Seattle, San Diego), Canada (Toronto, Ottawa, Edmonton), the United Kingdom (London, Birmingham, Bristol, Leicester, Manchester, Cardiff, Sheffield), Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy and Australia. Northern Somalis (from today's Somaliland) have a long history in Britain dating back to sailors in Cardiff and London in the late 1800s.

Links with home: remittances (xawaalad) from the diaspora are estimated at well over a billion US dollars a year, often around a quarter or more of GDP, and support families, businesses, education and emergency relief. Money is sent through hawala companies (Dahabshiil, Amal, Taaj, World Remit, etc.) and arrives in mobile money wallets. Many diaspora Somalis invest in real estate, hotels, telecoms and businesses, and some return to work in government; many Somali politicians hold or held foreign citizenship.

Diaspora identity: second-generation Somalis often speak a mix of Somali and the local language ("Somglish", "Swedali"), and some families send children to Somalia, Kenya or Somaliland for "dhaqan celis" (cultural rehabilitation), a controversial practice. Communities organise mosques, Somali schools, football tournaments (e.g. the Somali Week and community sports festivals), and associations. Somali-American politicians include US Representative Ilhan Omar (Minnesota).

Challenges discussed in the community: discrimination and Islamophobia, youth unemployment, mental health, immigration status and travel restrictions (for example US travel bans affecting Somali nationals, reinstated in June 2025), and the distance from ageing parents.

Assistant guidance: many users may be diaspora Somalis; they may switch between Somali and English, use non-standard spellings, and ask about both Somali and local systems (passports, visas, remittances, halal food, Islamic finance, schools). Answer for the country they are in, and avoid assuming they live in Somalia.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_diaspora; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_Americans; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_Somalia; https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/somalia/overview

knowledge.title: The Somali clan system: an overview for neutral discussion (Nidaamka qabiilka)
knowledge.text:
Somali society is organised by patrilineal descent groups, commonly called clans (qabiil, qolo, reer). Genealogy (abtirsiinyo, "counting ancestors") traces a person back through their father's line, and lineages are grouped into larger units. Scholars describe several levels: clan-family, clan, sub-clan, and the diya-paying group (mag-paying group) which is the most important unit for practical obligations.

Clan families as commonly described in the literature: the Darood (Daarood), Hawiye, Dir, Isaaq, and the Rahanweyn (Digil and Mirifle). Some sources count the Isaaq as part of the Dir, and some count Digil and Mirifle separately. In addition, Somalia includes minority communities such as the Bantu/Jareer (including Gosha and Shiidle communities along the rivers), Banaadiri (Reer Xamar, Reer Marka, Reer Baraawe), the Bajuni, and occupational groups such as Madhibaan, Tumaal and Yibir, who have historically faced discrimination.

Clans in politics: since 2000, power-sharing in federal institutions has used the "4.5 formula": equal shares for four major clan families (Darood, Hawiye, Dir, Digil-Mirifle) and half a share for a coalition of minorities. Critics say it entrenches clan identity and marginalises minorities; supporters say it ensured inclusion. Moves toward one-person-one-vote elections aim, in part, to move beyond it, but the debate continues (as of October 2026).

Important facts to keep in mind: clan identity is real and shapes marriage, conflict resolution, politics and solidarity, but Somalis also share one language, religion and culture, and many Somalis reject clannism (qabyaalad) as divisive. Clan has been associated with violence during the civil war, so the topic is sensitive and emotional.

Strict rules for an AI assistant:
1. Never ask a user what clan they belong to, and never guess it from their name, region or dialect.
2. Never rank clans, call any clan superior or inferior, or repeat stereotypes, jokes or insults about any clan or minority group.
3. Never take sides in clan conflicts, land disputes or clan-based political disputes; present documented facts neutrally and attribute claims ("X says…, Y says…").
4. If asked factual or academic questions (e.g. "what are the major clan families?"), answer briefly and neutrally as above, noting that classifications vary.
5. If a user expresses clan hatred or asks for content attacking a group, decline politely and steer to shared Somali identity and peace.
6. Do not produce genealogies for specific living people.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_clans; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4.5_formula; I.M. Lewis, A Pastoral Democracy (1961); https://www.refworld.org/reference/countryrep/euaa/2023/en/124196

knowledge.title: Xeer: Somali customary law and elders' mediation (Xeerka Soomaalida)
knowledge.text:
Xeer is the body of Somali customary law, an unwritten system of rules and precedents developed over centuries by clan elders (odayaal) to regulate relations between and within lineages. It operates alongside Islamic law (Sharia) and state law, and in many areas it remains the most used justice system, especially for family, land, livestock and conflict issues.

How xeer works:
- Elders as judges: disputes are heard by elders, sometimes in a council called shir or guurti, often under a tree. Respected elders with legal knowledge are called xeer-beegti (experts in xeer). Traditional leaders carry titles such as Suldaan, Ugaas, Garaad, Islaan, Boqor, Malaaq, depending on the community.
- Collective responsibility: a person's lineage (the mag-paying group) shares responsibility for compensation if a member injures or kills someone from another group, and receives compensation if a member is harmed.
- Negotiation and reconciliation: the aim is restoring peace between groups rather than punishing individuals. Settlement involves compensation, apologies and sometimes marriages between groups to cement peace.
- Protected categories: xeer traditionally protected certain people from violence in conflict, such as women, children, elderly, religious men (wadaad), guests, and envoys, sometimes described as "birmageydo" (those spared from the spear).
- Contractual agreements: groups made specific xeer agreements on grazing, wells, and alliances; these are renegotiated as circumstances change.

Xeer in modern governance: Somaliland institutionalised elders through its upper house, the Golaha Guurtida (House of Elders). Peace conferences that ended local wars (e.g. the Borama conference of 1993 in Somaliland and many local reconciliation meetings in the south) relied on xeer. Traditional elders also select federal MPs under the indirect electoral model used since 2012.

Critiques: human rights groups note that xeer can disadvantage women and minorities (for example, women do not sit as judges, and compensation may be paid to a family rather than to a victim), and that it sometimes conflicts with Sharia and state law, e.g. in cases of rape settled through compensation or marriage.

Assistant guidance: explain xeer neutrally as a living justice system; when a user has a dispute, describe options (elders, courts, Sharia courts, legal aid) without telling them which clan elders to approach; never encourage revenge.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xeer; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Elders_(Somaliland); Michael van Notten, The Law of the Somalis (2005); https://www.refworld.org/reference/countryrep/euaa/2023/en/124196

knowledge.title: Diya / Mag: blood compensation in Somali custom (Magta)
knowledge.text:
Mag (Arabic diya) is compensation paid for homicide or bodily injury. It is recognised in Islamic law and is a cornerstone of Somali xeer (customary law). In Somali custom, mag is paid collectively by the offender's mag-paying group (a lineage group of related men who have agreed to share such obligations) to the victim's group, which distributes it among relatives.

Amounts: the traditional full mag for the killing of a man is 100 camels (boqol geel), following classical Islamic jurisprudence. The full mag for a woman has traditionally been set at half (50 camels), a rule criticised by women's rights advocates. Injuries are compensated with fractions according to detailed customary scales (e.g. specific amounts for the loss of an eye or limb). Today mag is usually paid in US dollars calculated from current camel values, and the cash amount varies by region and agreement; figures in the tens of thousands of dollars are commonly reported for a full mag. Exact amounts are negotiated by elders and should not be presented as fixed.

Process: after a killing, elders of both sides meet quickly to prevent revenge (aano / aarsi). The offender's side may make an initial payment or gesture to show good faith and open talks. Accidental killings (e.g. road accidents) are also handled through mag, which is why traffic accidents in Somalia are often settled by elders. Deliberate murder can lead to demands for qisaas (retribution) under Sharia, though families can accept mag instead; courts in Somalia and Somaliland apply Sharia-based penal law alongside customary settlements.

Social role: the collective mag system creates strong mutual obligations: members contribute when someone in their group causes harm and receive help when they are harmed. It discourages violence by making the whole group pay, but critics say it can shield individual offenders from personal accountability.

Assistant guidance: describe mag factually and neutrally if asked; never advise someone to seek revenge; for an actual case, suggest involving elders, police, courts and legal aid together, and do not state specific monetary amounts as binding.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diyya; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xeer; I.M. Lewis, A Pastoral Democracy (1961); https://www.refworld.org/reference/countryrep/euaa/2023/en/124196

knowledge.title: Ancient Somali history: Land of Punt, Laas Geel and coastal city-states (Taariikhda hore)
knowledge.text:
The Somali peninsula has a very long human history. Rock art at Laas Geel (Laas Geel), near Hargeysa, discovered by a French archaeological team in 2002, shows painted cattle and people in ceremonial dress and is estimated to be roughly 5,000 years old or more; it is among the best-preserved rock art sites in Africa. Other ancient sites include Dhambalin and Karin Heegan.

Land of Punt: Ancient Egyptian records from about 2500 BCE onward describe trade expeditions to "Punt", a land rich in incense (frankincense and myrrh), ebony, gold, ivory and exotic animals. The most famous expedition was sent by Queen Hatshepsut around 1470 BCE and is depicted on her temple at Deir el-Bahari. Scholars debate Punt's exact location: many place it along the southern Red Sea and Horn of Africa coast, including northern Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea and parts of Sudan and Ethiopia. Somalis often identify Punt with their land, and the name "Puntland" (adopted in 1998) draws on that heritage. An assistant should say "possibly included" rather than presenting Punt as definitely Somali.

Classical antiquity: the Greek merchant guide "Periplus of the Erythraean Sea" (1st century CE) describes trading ports along the "Barbaria" coast, such as Malao (often identified with Berbera), Mundus, Mosylon, and Opone (identified with sites near Xaafuun/Hafun). Somali ports traded frankincense, myrrh, cinnamon and animal products with Egypt, Arabia, Persia, India and Rome. The Horn of Africa remains the world's main source of frankincense (from Boswellia trees in the Cal Madow and Bari regions) and myrrh.

Early Islamic period: from the 7th century Islam spread along the coast. By the 10th–13th centuries, Mogadishu (Muqdisho), Marka, Baraawe and Zeila (Saylac) were wealthy Muslim trading cities. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited Mogadishu in 1331 and described its sultan, generous hospitality and fine cloth exports. Mogadishu minted its own coins under the Muqdisho Sultanate. Zeila was a major port linking the Ethiopian highlands to Arabia.

The Somali language and people: Somali is a Cushitic language, related to Oromo, Afar and others. Somali oral genealogies and Arabic sources trace the presence of Somali-speaking pastoralists across the Horn over many centuries.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laas_Geel; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_Punt; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periplus_of_the_Erythraean_Sea; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Somalia

knowledge.title: The Adal Sultanate and Imam Ahmad Gurey (Saldanadda Cadal iyo Axmed Gurey)
knowledge.text:
The Adal Sultanate (Saldanadda Cadal) was a Muslim state in the Horn of Africa that flourished from about 1415 to 1577. It succeeded the earlier Sultanate of Ifat (Ifaat), whose Walashma dynasty was defeated by the Christian Ethiopian (Abyssinian) kingdom. Adal's territory covered much of today's Somaliland, Djibouti, the Somali Region and eastern Ethiopia; its early capital was Dakkar and later Harar (Harar), and the port of Zeila (Saylac) was its main gateway for trade with Arabia, Egypt and India. Adal's population included Somali, Afar, Harari, Argobba and other Muslim peoples.

Adal fought a long series of wars with the Ethiopian Empire. The most famous leader was Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (c. 1506–1543), known in Somali as Axmed Gurey ("Ahmed the left-handed"; Amharic "Gragn"). From 1529, after victory at the Battle of Shimbra Kure, his forces conquered much of the Ethiopian highlands in a campaign known as the "Conquest of Abyssinia" (Futuh al-Habasha, chronicled in Arabic by Shihab al-Din). His armies included many Somali contingents, and they used firearms and cannons obtained with Ottoman help. Portugal sent a force under Cristóvão da Gama to aid Ethiopia; Imam Ahmad was killed at the Battle of Wayna Daga in 1543, and Adal's power declined. His widow Bati del Wambara encouraged continued resistance, and his nephew Emir Nur ibn Mujahid built the walls of Harar.

Legacy: Axmed Gurey is a national hero to many Somalis (a main street and monuments in Mogadishu were named after him, and he is celebrated in Somali nationalism), while in Ethiopian history he is remembered as a destructive invader. An assistant should present both perspectives neutrally. After Adal's decline, the region saw the Oromo migrations, and power shifted to the Emirate of Harar and to smaller Somali sultanates.

Key facts: Adal Sultanate c. 1415–1577; capitals Dakkar then Harar; port Zeila; leader Imam Ahmad Gurey (died 1543); main source Futuh al-Habasha.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adal_Sultanate; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_ibn_Ibrahim_al-Ghazi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ifat_Sultanate; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futuh_al-Habasha

knowledge.title: Ajuran, Geledi, Majeerteen, Hobyo and Isaaq sultanates (Saldanadihii Soomaaliyeed)
knowledge.text:
Between the 13th and 19th centuries several Somali states rose in the interior and on the coast.

Ajuran Sultanate (Saldanadda Ajuuraan, c. 13th–late 17th century): a powerful state in southern Somalia controlling the Shabeelle and Jubba river valleys and the Benadir coast (Mogadishu, Marka, Baraawe). It was known for hydraulic engineering: wells, cisterns and irrigation canals, and taxed water and farm produce. Ajuran traded with Arabia, Persia, India, China (Ming-dynasty contacts) and the Ottomans, and resisted Portuguese attacks on the coast in the 16th century. It declined in the late 1600s due to internal revolts and was succeeded by smaller states.

Geledi Sultanate (Saldanadda Geledi, late 17th–19th century): based at Afgooye on the Shabeelle River, ruled by the Gobroon dynasty. Under Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim and later Sultan Ahmed Yusuf, it dominated the southern interior and the Benadir trade, defeating rival forces at the Battle of Bardheere (1843). It had a large agricultural economy, partly based on slave labour of Bantu communities, which is part of the historical background to the marginalisation of the Somali Bantu (Jareer). The Geledi signed treaties with Italy in the late 19th century and were absorbed into Italian Somaliland.

Majeerteen Sultanate (Migiurtinia, mid-18th century–1927): in the north-east (today's Puntland), ruled by Boqor Cismaan Maxamuud in the late 19th century from Aluula and Bargaal. It traded frankincense and controlled the north-east coast; it signed protectorate treaties with Italy (1889) but kept autonomy until conquered by Italian Fascist forces in 1927.

Sultanate of Hobyo (Saldanadda Hobyo, 1878–1926): founded by Yuusuf Cali Keenadiid (Yusuf Ali Kenadid), a relative and rival of Boqor Cismaan, at Hobyo on the central coast. His son Cismaan Yuusuf Keenadiid invented the Osmanya script (Far Soomaali) for writing Somali in the 1920s. Hobyo was annexed by Italy in 1925–1926.

Isaaq Sultanate (18th century–1884): in the north-west (today's Somaliland), led by Sultans of the Guled dynasty, based around Toon and later Hargeysa; it signed treaties with Britain in the 1880s.

Other states included the Warsangali Sultanate (Sanaag) and the Sultanate of the Mudug and Gedo areas. Assistant guidance: describe these states factually; avoid presenting any one as the "real" Somali state, as each is linked to particular communities today.

knowledge.title: Colonial partition of Somali lands (Gumeysiga: British, Italian, French, Ethiopian)
knowledge.text:
In the late 19th century the Somali-inhabited Horn of Africa was divided among Britain, Italy, France and the Ethiopian Empire; the Somali star on the flag (five points) symbolises these five territories.

British Somaliland (Somaliland Protectorate, 1884/1887–1960): Britain signed treaties with northern clans from 1884 and declared a protectorate in 1887, mainly to supply meat to its garrison in Aden. The capital moved from Berbera to Hargeysa in 1941. Rule was light ("indirect"); the main resistance came from the Dervish movement (1899–1920). Italy briefly occupied it in August 1940 during World War II, and Britain retook it in 1941.

Italian Somaliland (Somalia Italiana, 1889–1941): Italy acquired the Benadir coast through treaties with local sultans and by leasing ports from the Sultan of Zanzibar, and later conquered the north-eastern sultanates (1925–1927). Mogadishu was the capital. Italy developed banana and sugar plantations along the rivers using forced labour, and Fascist rule was harsh. Britain occupied it in 1941; after World War II the UN made it the Trust Territory of Somalia under Italian administration (AFIS, 1950–1960) with a ten-year deadline for independence.

French Somaliland (Côte française des Somalis, 1883/1896–1967): around the port of Djibouti, inhabited by Somali (mainly Issa) and Afar communities. Renamed the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas in 1967, it became independent as the Republic of Djibouti on 27 June 1977, choosing not to join Somalia.

Northern Frontier District (NFD) of Kenya: the British colony of Kenya included a large Somali-inhabited region. In 1962 a British commission found most residents favoured union with Somalia, but Britain transferred the NFD to independent Kenya in 1963, leading to the Shifta War (1963–1967). The area is now mainly Garissa, Wajir and Mandera counties.

Ogaden and the Haud (Ethiopia): Ethiopia under Emperor Menelik II expanded into Somali-inhabited lands in the 1890s; Anglo-Ethiopian treaties of 1897 recognised Ethiopian claims. Britain administered the Ogaden after World War II but returned it to Ethiopia in 1948, and the Haud grazing area in 1954, causing great anger among Somalis. Today it forms Ethiopia's Somali Region. Somalia's claim led to the 1964 border war and the 1977–1978 Ogaden War.

Assistant guidance: describe these borders and claims factually; questions of "Greater Somalia" (Soomaaliweyn) are political and should be presented as history and opinion, not as an assistant's position.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Somaliland; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Somaliland; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Somaliland; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Frontier_District

knowledge.title: The Dervish movement and Sayid Maxamed Cabdulle Xasan (Daraawiishta)
knowledge.text:
The Dervish State (Dawladdii Daraawiishta) was an anti-colonial movement and polity in the northern Somali territories that fought British, Italian and Ethiopian forces from 1899 to 1920. Its leader was Sayid Maxamed Cabdulle Xasan (Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, c. 1856–1920), a religious scholar of the Saalixiya Sufi order, a famous poet, and a central figure in Somali nationalism. British officials called him "the Mad Mullah", a term Somalis consider insulting; an assistant should use his proper name or "the Sayid".

Rise: after studying in Mecca and returning to Berbera around 1895, the Sayid preached against colonial influence and Christian missionaries. In 1899 he declared jihad against the British and gathered followers (daraawiish, from "dervish") from many clans. His forces won major victories, notably at Gumburu and Daratoleh (1903) and at Dul Madoba (1913), where the British Camel Constabulary under Richard Corfield was defeated and Corfield killed. The Sayid's poem about Corfield's death is one of the most famous in the language.

State and forts: the Dervishes built stone forts, notably at Taleex (Taleh) in today's Sool region, which served as their capital, and at Jidali and Illig. The movement also caused great suffering among Somali communities who opposed it, and it fought internal Somali rivals as well as colonial armies. Historians note both its anti-colonial heroism and its violence against other Somalis.

Defeat: in January–February 1920, Britain launched a combined air and ground campaign; Royal Air Force aircraft bombed Taleex and other forts, one of the first uses of air power in colonial warfare in Africa. The Sayid escaped to the Ogaden and died of illness (reportedly influenza) in Imey in December 1920.

Poetry: the Sayid is regarded as one of the greatest Somali poets (gabayaa), using gabay poetry as propaganda, rebuke and inspiration. Lines from his poems are widely memorised. Modern Somali governments made him a national hero: a statue stood in Mogadishu, and many institutions bear his name.

Assistant guidance: present him as a national hero to many Somalis and also note historical controversy where relevant; never mock him or use the colonial nickname except when explaining it.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Abdullah_Hassan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dervish_movement_(Somali); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taleh; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dul_Madoba

knowledge.title: Independence and the civilian republic, 1960–1969 (Xorriyadda iyo dawladdii rayidka)
knowledge.text:
Somali independence came in two steps in 1960. On 26 June 1960, the British Somaliland Protectorate became independent as the State of Somaliland, recognised by about 35 countries. On 1 July 1960, the UN Trust Territory of Somalia (former Italian Somaliland) became independent, and the two united the same day to form the Somali Republic (Jamhuuriyadda Soomaaliyeed), with Mogadishu as capital. The flag, a white five-pointed star on light blue (designed by Mohammed Awale Liban and adopted in 1954), was raised. The Somali Youth League (SYL, Leegada), founded in 1943, was the leading nationalist party.

Leaders: Aden Abdullah Osman Daar (Aadan Cabdulle Cismaan, "Aadan Cadde") was the first president (1960–1967); Abdirashid Ali Shermarke (Cabdirashiid Cali Sharmaarke) was the first prime minister. In 1967 Shermarke was elected president and Mohamed Haji Ibrahim Egal (Maxamed Xaaji Ibraahim Cigaal) became prime minister. Aadan Cadde became the first African president to peacefully hand over power after losing an election, a point of Somali pride.

Politics: the 1961 constitutional referendum was approved nationally but rejected by many voters in the north, an early sign of northern dissatisfaction with the union. The republic was a parliamentary democracy with many clan-based parties; the 1969 election had over 60 parties. Corruption and clan patronage grew.

Foreign affairs: the government pursued Pan-Somalism, the goal of uniting all Somali territories (Soomaaliweyn), which led to conflict with Ethiopia (1964 border war) and Kenya (Shifta War, 1963–1967). Prime Minister Egal pursued détente with both neighbours from 1967.

End of the republic: on 15 October 1969, President Shermarke was assassinated by one of his bodyguards in Laascaanood. On 21 October 1969, the army, led by Major General Mohamed Siad Barre (Maxamed Siyaad Barre), seized power in a bloodless coup, suspended the constitution, dissolved parliament and created the Supreme Revolutionary Council. The country was renamed the Somali Democratic Republic.

Assistant guidance: 26 June and 1 July are public holidays; describe the 1960 union as a fact, and note that Somaliland today interprets its 26 June independence as the basis of its claim, while the Federal Government regards the union as permanent.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_Republic; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Somaliland; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Abdullah_Osman_Daar; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdirashid_Ali_Shermarke

knowledge.title: The Siad Barre era, 1969–1991 (Xilligii Kacaanka iyo Maxamed Siyaad Barre)
knowledge.text:
Mohamed Siad Barre (Maxamed Siyaad Barre, c. 1919–1995) ruled Somalia from the coup of 21 October 1969 until January 1991. His government called itself "Kacaan" (the Revolution) and he was called "Jaalle Siyaad" (Comrade Siad).

Early period and achievements claimed: the regime adopted "scientific socialism" (hantiwadaag cilmiga ku dhisan), nationalised banks and businesses, and allied with the Soviet Union. On 21 October 1972 it adopted the Latin-based Somali alphabet as the official script, making Somali the official language of government and schooling. Mass literacy campaigns (Ololihii Horumarinta Reer Miyiga, 1974–1975) sent students to teach in rural areas, and literacy rose sharply. The regime also expanded schools, built roads and the national theatre, and promoted national culture, including the Waaberi troupe. A 1975 Family Law gave women equal inheritance rights, which drew opposition from religious scholars; ten scholars were executed in 1975 for protesting it. Somalia joined the Arab League in 1974. The 1974–1975 "Dabadheer" drought was met with resettlement programmes.

Ogaden War (1977–1978): Somalia invaded Ethiopia's Ogaden in support of the Western Somali Liberation Front, initially capturing most of the region. The Soviet Union and Cuba switched sides to back Ethiopia, and Somalia was defeated in March 1978. Somalia then aligned with the United States. The defeat brought a flood of refugees and the start of armed opposition.

Repression and opposition: the regime increasingly relied on loyal clans, secret police (NSS) and the military. Armed opposition groups formed: the Somali Salvation Democratic Front (SSDF, 1978), the Somali National Movement (SNM, 1981) in the north, the United Somali Congress (USC, 1989) and the Somali Patriotic Movement (SPM). In 1988, after the SNM attacked Hargeysa and Burco, government forces bombed and shelled both cities, killing many thousands of civilians and displacing hundreds of thousands. Many in Somaliland describe the 1987–1989 killings of Isaaq civilians as genocide (the "Hargeisa Holocaust"); a UN-commissioned report in 2001 used that term, and the issue remains deeply painful.

Fall: by 1990 the government controlled little beyond Mogadishu. On 26 January 1991 Siad Barre fled the capital as USC forces advanced; he died in exile in Lagos, Nigeria, in 1995.

Assistant guidance: views of the era differ sharply. Some remember order, literacy and national pride; others remember dictatorship, repression and mass atrocities. Present both factually, and treat the 1988 events with gravity.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siad_Barre; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogaden_War; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaaq_genocide; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_Democratic_Republic

knowledge.title: State collapse and civil war, 1991–2000 (Burburkii dawladda iyo dagaalladii sokeeye)
knowledge.text:
After Siad Barre fled Mogadishu on 26 January 1991, the central state collapsed. The victorious United Somali Congress split between factions led by General Mohamed Farah Aidid (Maxamed Faarax Caydiid) and Ali Mahdi Mohamed (Cali Mahdi Maxamed), who was declared interim president. Their fighting devastated Mogadishu in 1991–1992, dividing it along the "Green Line". Militias controlled by warlords (dagaal-ooge) fought for territory across the south.

Famine and international intervention: fighting and drought in 1991–1992 caused a famine that killed an estimated 200,000–300,000 people, concentrated in the Bay and Bakool region (Baydhabo was called the "city of death"). The UN launched UNOSOM I in 1992, followed by the US-led UNITAF ("Operation Restore Hope", December 1992), and then UNOSOM II (1993–1995). In June 1993, Pakistani peacekeepers were killed, and the UN pursued Aidid. On 3–4 October 1993, the Battle of Mogadishu ("Black Hawk Down") left 18 US soldiers and many hundreds of Somalis dead. The US withdrew in March 1994 and the UN by March 1995.

Somaliland and Puntland: in the north-west, the SNM and clan elders met at the Grand Conference of the Northern Peoples in Burco and declared the Republic of Somaliland on 18 May 1991, restoring the borders of the former British Somaliland. In the north-east, the Puntland State of Somalia was founded on 1 August 1998 at a conference in Garoowe, with Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed as its first president; Puntland describes itself as an autonomous part of Somalia.

The south: after 1995, Mogadishu and the south remained divided among factions, with local Islamic courts emerging in Mogadishu neighbourhoods in the late 1990s to provide order. Many peace conferences failed (e.g. Addis Ababa 1993, Sodere 1996, Cairo 1997). Despite the war, private businesses—telecoms, money transfer (xawaalad), aviation and trade—grew rapidly without state regulation.

Human cost: hundreds of thousands were killed or died of famine, and over a million fled abroad, creating the modern Somali diaspora and large refugee camps in Kenya (Dadaab, opened in 1991) and Ethiopia.

Assistant guidance: avoid blaming any clan collectively for the civil war; attribute actions to named factions and leaders; be sensitive, as many users lost relatives during this period.
